---
title: "Teaching"
---

Theory disciplines the evidence, the evidence tests the theory, and students learn best when they work with both. In my courses, students read the research behind the textbook and then make a case of their own---taking a country's development record, for instance, and defending a policy response before the class.

## Courses Taught

I was the instructor of record for four undergraduate courses at George Mason University from 2021 to 2024, in person and online, designing the syllabus, assignments, and exams for each.

**ECON 104: Principles of Macroeconomics** [Summer 2024 · Online]{.aside}

An introduction to thinking like an economist about the whole economy, built around a few big questions: why some nations are rich and others poor, what the Federal Reserve does, and why economies go through business cycles.

**ECON 306: Intermediate Microeconomics** [Fall 2023 · Online]{.aside}

Price theory at the intermediate level: consumer choice and demand, production and costs, and how market structure shapes prices and output, practiced through weekly problem sets with an emphasis on graphical analysis.

**ECON 360: Economics of Developing Areas** [Spring 2023, Summer 2022 · In person]{.aside}

Why are some countries rich and others poor? The course moves from Malthus and Solow through poverty traps, the aid debate, health and human capital, institutions, culture, state capacity, and conflict, pairing Easterly, Banerjee and Duflo, and Koyama and Rubin with research by North, Nunn, Dell, and others. Students write discussion essays and present a country case.

**ECON 385: International Economic Policy** [Spring 2022, Fall 2021 · In person]{.aside}

The economic way of thinking applied to trade and international finance, including introductory microeconomics and game theory, with historical and current evidence on the consequences of trade, protectionism, and conflict. Taught for non-major students.

## Courses I Would Like to Teach

I am prepared to teach principles and intermediate micro- and macroeconomics, undergraduate econometrics, economic development, and economic history---with notice. I would also like to build courses of my own:

**Institutions and Historical Political Economy**

<!-- ::: {.callout collapse="true" title="Description"}
Why do some societies build institutions that sustain growth and order, while others stall or fall into conflict? This upper-level course pairs the theory of states, violence, and institutional change with the empirical economic history that tests it: climate, ancient conflict, meideval guilds and city councils, representative assemblies, colonial institutions, and the long shadow they cast on present-day outcomes. Its centerpiece is a replication exercise: students reproduce a published historical result from the original data, then probe whether it survives a change of their own design.
::: -->

**Building Evidence from the Historical Record**

<!-- ::: {.callout collapse="true" title="Description"}
Most claims about the past were made before anyone could test them with data. This methods seminar teaches students to build the evidence themselves: digitizing and coding primary sources, constructing geo-referenced panels, and finding credible variation in observational data. Working from a shared dataset drawn from my own research---digitized nineteenth-century newspapers or geocoded episodes of medieval unrest---students move through the full pipeline from raw source to defensible result, and leave with a finished piece of original research. No prior programming experience is assumed.
::: -->
